etymology: From the Aramaic reyqa', “empty one, worthless fellow,” from a root signifying “to be empty, void, vain”; carried untranslated through the Greek of Matthew into the KJV, whose margin renders it “Vain fellow.”
biblical_def: Raca is a word of contempt — the Aramaic sneer that calls a man empty, a worthless nothing, a head with nothing in it. Our Lord takes it up in the Sermon on the Mount, where He drives the sixth commandment past the hand and into the heart. The scribes had heard it said by them of old time, “Thou shalt not kill” (Mat 5:21), and had made the law a fence about the outward act only: keep your knife sheathed and you are guiltless. Christ answers that the commandment reaches further than any court of men can follow. “Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire” (Mat 5:22). Here is a rising scale — the anger nursed, the contempt spoken, the scorn that damns the soul — and every rung of it is murder in the sight of God. To call a brother Raca is to unmake him, to strike the image of God in him with the tongue, to pass a sentence of worthlessness upon one whom the LORD may have chosen from before the foundation of the world. Our Lord traces the whole traffic to its spring: “out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders” (Mat 15:19). The murderer’s work begins long before the blow, in the contempt that first empties a brother of his worth.
webster_summary: A term of contempt: empty one, worthless fellow; the Aramaic sneer our Lord names as murder of the heart.
webster_full: RACA, a Syriac or Aramaic word of contempt, signifying empty, vain, worthless.
The KJV margin renders it “Vain fellow” (Mat 5:22).
It is a sneer that pronounces a brother of no account.
Our Lord ranks it with murder under the sixth commandment.
It is spoken by the tongue but conceived in the heart (Mat 15:19).
scriptures: Mat 5:21
Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:
Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:
Jas 3:9
Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.
corruption_summary: The age reduces the sixth commandment to bare outward murder; Christ Himself extends it to the angry heart and the contemptuous tongue.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is ancient and thoroughly modern at once: the reduction of the sixth commandment to the bare outward act. The scribes taught that a man who had shed no blood had kept the law, and the age agrees with them — it reckons itself innocent of murder because it has never lifted a hand, while it slays with the tongue daily and calls the slaughter opinion. Christ forecloses that defence. He puts the anger, the Raca, and the “Thou fool” on one continuous ladder with the knife, and hangs hell fire at the end of it. The law of God is spiritual; it binds the heart, and no man who has despised his brother may plead a clean hand.

The sneer is a doctrine as well as a sin. To say Raca is to declare a man empty — a nothing, of no account, worthless — and that is a lie against Genesis 1:27, for the brother so dismissed bears the image of God, and may be a vessel of mercy afore prepared unto glory. James marks the contradiction: with the same tongue we bless God and curse men, which are made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9). The remedy is not a stricter guard upon the lips but a new heart, out of which the evil thought no longer proceeds. Christ, who was Himself despised and rejected, took the contempt of men upon the tree; the sinner who has said Raca to his brother must go to Him for pardon, and having been pardoned, learn to see his brother as God sees him.
roots_summary: The word means an empty one, a worthless fellow — a spoken sneer of contempt.
roots_lines: Raca — from the Aramaic reyqa', “empty, vain, worthless.”
It is left untranslated in the Greek text and in the KJV.
The KJV margin explains it: “Vain fellow.”
It names a brother as a nothing, a head with nothing in it.
Christ ranks it with murder under the sixth commandment (Mat 5:22).
usage: To say Raca is to call a brother empty — and to strike the image of God with the tongue.
The sixth commandment reaches past the hand to the angry heart and the contemptuous word.
Anger, Raca, and “Thou fool” are rungs of one ladder, and hell fire hangs at the end.

etymology: From the Greek tetrarchēs, from tetra (“four”) and archē (“rule, dominion”); properly the ruler of a fourth part of a region, and by Roman usage a petty prince under the emperor, lower in dignity than a king. The KJV margin glosses it “governor over four provinces.”
biblical_def: A tetrarch is the ruler of a fourth part — a princeling set over a portion of a divided kingdom, holding his little authority at the pleasure of Rome. When Herod the Great died, his realm was parcelled out, and the New Testament’s tetrarchs are the sons and successors who governed the fragments. Luke, writing as an historian and not a fabulist, anchors the coming of the word of God to John in the exact machinery of that government: “in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea… and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene” (Luk 3:1). The gospel did not fall out of the sky into a myth; it entered a dated world of named rulers whose reigns can be counted. Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, is the man the word haunts. He shut John in prison and took his head; and when the fame of Jesus reached him, “he was perplexed” (Luk 9:7), and “said unto his servants, This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead” (Mat 14:1-2). A guilty conscience is a poor counsellor, and the tetrarch who silenced the preacher could not silence the sermon. Yet grace ran through that very household: among the prophets and teachers at Antioch was “Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch” (Act 13:1). The foster-brother was saved; the tetrarch perished. Election, not proximity, makes the difference.
webster_summary: A ruler of a fourth part of a province or kingdom; a petty prince under Rome, lower in dignity than a king.
webster_full: TETRARCH, a Roman governor of the fourth part of a province or kingdom.
From the Greek tetra, “four,” and archē, “rule.”
The KJV margin: “governor over four provinces” (Mat 14:1).
Herod Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee, Philip of Ituraea, Lysanias of Abilene (Luk 3:1).
The title marks a borrowed authority, held at the pleasure of Caesar.
scriptures: Mat 14:1
At that time Herod the tetrarch heard of the fame of Jesus,
Luk 3:1

Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene,
Luk 9:7
Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead;
Act 13:1

Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition presses on the word; it recovers that the gospel entered a dated world of named rulers, and that nearness to Christ is not grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The title itself preaches a sermon on borrowed authority. A tetrarch is not a king; he is a fourth of one, a man ruling a fragment by the sufferance of a greater throne, and every honour he has is lent. Herod Antipas played the prince, silenced the preacher who reproved him, and took John’s head to keep an oath sworn at a birthday feast — and could not keep his own conscience. When the fame of Jesus came to him he was perplexed, and feared that the Baptist was risen. The man who can command a headsman cannot command his own heart at midnight. All earthly rule is tetrarchy: a portion, held briefly, under the King of kings, to whom the account is owed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, Luke’s dating: he sets the word of God to John in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with Pilate governing and three tetrarchs named to their districts. The canonical narrative is authoritative history, and the coins and inscriptions that name these same men are corroboration, not permission to believe. Second, the household of Herod. Manaen was brought up with the tetrarch and stood at Antioch a prophet of the church; Herod heard John gladly for a season and died an apostate. Two men reared under one roof, one taken and one left. Nearness to the preacher, the palace, or even the pulpit saves no man; the effectual call of God does.
roots_summary: The word means the ruler of a fourth part — a petty prince beneath a king.
roots_lines: Tetrarch — Greek tetrarchēs, from tetra + archē.
It denotes the ruler of a fourth part of a divided realm.
Herod the Great’s kingdom was parcelled out among such rulers.
The KJV margin glosses it “governor over four provinces.”
Luke names three tetrarchs to date the coming of the word to John (Luk 3:1).
usage: A tetrarch rules a fourth part — all earthly authority is borrowed and briefly held.
Luke dates the gospel by living tetrarchs: this history happened, in a year men could count.
Manaen was reared with the tetrarch and preached at Antioch; Herod heard John and perished.

etymology: From the Greek alabastron, a flask or cruse of alabaster — a soft, translucent stone quarried in Egypt and worked into narrow-necked vessels which kept costly ointment from spoiling; the neck was sealed and had to be broken to pour.
biblical_def: An alabaster box is not a chest but a flask — a slender vessel cut from soft white stone, sealed at the neck, in which precious ointment was kept from the air. Because the neck was broken to pour, the flask could be spent but once; the giving was total by the very make of the thing. Three times a woman brings such a box to Christ. In the house of Simon the Pharisee, “a woman in the city, which was a sinner… brought an alabaster box of ointment” (Luk 7:37), and washed His feet with tears. In Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman “having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious… brake the box, and poured it on his head” (Mar 14:3; Mat 26:7). She did not measure a portion and cork the rest for another day. She broke it. Nothing was reserved, and the whole house was filled with the odour. The objection came at once, and it came from the disciples: “To what purpose is this waste?” (Mat 26:8). Judas priced the ointment at three hundred pence and spoke of the poor. But our Lord defended her: “she hath wrought a good work on me… she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.” The broken flask was a preaching of the broken body. What is poured out on Christ is never waste; it is the only spending that heaven records, and He promised her memorial wherever the gospel should be preached.
webster_summary: A flask of alabaster stone holding precious ointment, sealed at the neck and broken to pour; the vessel of extravagant worship at Bethany.
webster_full: ALABASTER BOX, a cruse or flask of alabaster, a soft white translucent stone.
Such vessels preserved costly ointments from the air.
The narrow neck was sealed, and had to be broken before the ointment could be poured.
A woman brake such a box upon the head of Christ at Bethany (Mar 14:3).
A woman that was a sinner brought one to His feet in the Pharisee’s house (Luk 7:37).
scriptures: Mat 26:7
There came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat.
Mar 14:3

And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head.
Luk 7:37
And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment,
Mat 26:8
But when his disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose is this waste?
corruption_summary: The utilitarian objection — “to what purpose is this waste?” — still reckons costly worship a squandering better spent elsewhere.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is spoken in the text itself, and it wears a benevolent face: “To what purpose is this waste? For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor.” It is Judas’s arithmetic, and the age has learned it by heart. Whatever is spent on the worship of God — the hours, the substance, the beauty, the best of a life poured out with nothing kept back — is arraigned as inefficiency, and a ledger is produced to prove that it might have done more good elsewhere. John notes that Judas said this not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief; and the modern calculus that reduces the church to a distributor of relief and calls adoration wasteful is very often the same heart, with a better reputation. Christ has never yet accepted the objection.

Mark the answer, for it settles the account. “Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me.” The poor ye have always with you, but Christ was going to His burial, and she alone had understood it. Her worship was not a subtraction from mercy but the fountain of it: no man loves the poor rightly who has not first broken his flask over the head of Christ. And the flask had to be broken — there is no pouring while the neck is sealed and the ointment safe. A worship that costs nothing and risks nothing and reserves the remainder for a better occasion is not worship at all. The Lord took her deed into the gospel itself, that wherever it is preached, this also should be told for a memorial of her.
roots_summary: The word means a sealed flask of alabaster stone, broken open to pour out precious ointment.
roots_lines: Alabaster — Greek alabastron, a flask cut from soft white stone.
The stone was quarried in Egypt and worked into narrow-necked vessels.
The sealed neck kept costly ointment from spoiling.
To pour, the box had to be broken — the gift could not be halved.
At Bethany the woman brake the box on Christ’s head (Mar 14:3).
usage: She brake the box: the neck must be broken before the ointment can be poured.
“To what purpose is this waste?” is Judas’s arithmetic, and Christ overruled it.
What is poured out upon Christ is never waste; He wrote her memorial into the gospel.

etymology: From the Old French nappe, “a cloth,” with the diminutive -kin; the KJV’s rendering of the Greek soudarion (a Latin loan, sudarium, “sweat-cloth”) — a small cloth for the face, used to wipe the brow, to wrap a treasure, or to bind the head of the dead.
biblical_def: A napkin in the KJV is no table-linen but a small face-cloth — the sudarium, a hand’s breadth of fabric put to four uses in the New Testament, and every one of them instructive. It is the sloth’s hiding-place: the wicked servant returns his master’s money untraded, “Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin” (Luk 19:20) — the talent not squandered but wrapped, which is condemnation enough, for buried faithfulness is unfaithfulness. It is the badge of death: Lazarus came forth from the tomb bound hand and foot with graveclothes, “and his face was bound about with a napkin” (Joh 11:44), and had to be loosed, for he was raised only to die again. It is a channel of apostolic power: from Paul’s body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs and aprons (Act 19:12), the same word, in an age of signs now closed. But the napkin’s glory is in the empty tomb. Peter went in and saw the linen clothes lie, “and the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself” (Joh 20:7). It was not torn away, not tumbled, not carried off — it was folded and set apart, in the calm of One who had risen at leisure. Lazarus needed loosing; Christ left His grave-cloth behind Him in order, and the disciple that saw it believed.
webster_summary: A small face-cloth (the Greek soudarion): used to wrap a treasure, to bind the head of the dead, and folded by itself in the empty tomb.
webster_full: NAPKIN, a cloth for wiping the face; from the Old French nappe, “a cloth.”
It renders the Greek soudarion, from the Latin sudarium, a “sweat-cloth.”
In it the slothful servant hid his lord’s pound (Luk 19:20).
With it the face of the dead was bound about (Joh 11:44).
In the empty tomb it lay wrapped together in a place by itself (Joh 20:7).
scriptures: And another came, saying, Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin:
And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
Joh 20:7
And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.
corruption_summary: The stolen-body theory, urged since Reimarus and the rationalists, is answered by a folded cloth: thieves do not tidy a grave.
corruption_paragraphs: The rationalist denial of the resurrection is as old as the guards at the sepulchre, who were paid to say, “His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept” (Mat 28:13), and it was revived in the eighteenth century by Reimarus and the deists as the fraud hypothesis, which every generation of unbelief has since refurbished. The napkin answers it. A body snatched in haste by thieves in the dark is carried off wrapped, or the wrappings are torn away and flung down; what no robber does is unwind a hundred pound weight of spice-laden linen, leave it lying in its place, and then fold the face-cloth and set it apart by itself. The evidence in that tomb is not the evidence of theft; it is the evidence of a Man who rose from the dead without hurry and left the room in order. John looked at that folded cloth, and he believed.

The napkin also parts the two risings. Lazarus came out of his tomb still bound, his face bound about with a napkin, and had to be loosed by other men — a resuscitation, and a borrowed one; he wore his grave-clothes out of the grave because he would need them again. Christ left His behind. He passed out of the linen as He would pass through the doors, and the sweat-cloth of His dying lay folded where His head had been, a flag of a finished work. And the servant’s napkin at Luke 19 is the last warning: what is wrapped and laid up is not kept safe but lost. The Lord’s pound is given to be traded, and the man who folds his gift away in a cloth will find that the folding was the sin.
roots_summary: The word means a small face-cloth — the Greek soudarion, a sweat-cloth.
roots_lines: Napkin — Old French nappe, “a cloth,” with the diminutive -kin.
It renders the Greek soudarion, from the Latin sudarium.
It denotes a small cloth for the face, not table-linen.
The slothful servant wrapped his lord’s pound in one (Luk 19:20).
In the empty tomb it lay folded in a place by itself (Joh 20:7).
usage: The pound kept laid up in a napkin was not kept safe but lost — buried faithfulness is unfaithfulness.
Lazarus came forth bound, his face bound about with a napkin, and had to be loosed.
The napkin lay folded by itself: thieves do not tidy a grave, and John believed.

etymology: From the Old French mangeoire, “an eating-place,” from manger (“to eat”), from the Latin manducare, “to chew”; hence the trough or crib from which cattle feed. It renders the Greek phatnē.
biblical_def: A manger is a feeding-trough — the crib out of which oxen and asses eat, hollowed of stone or timber, standing where the beasts are stalled. It is the plainest furniture of a working world, and Luke names it three times in fourteen verses, because the Holy Ghost would have us stare at it. “She brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7). The angel makes the trough the very token of the Saviour: “this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger” (Luk 2:12) — not a palace, not a guard, not a star over a cradle of gold; you shall know the Christ of God by the cattle’s crib. And the shepherds “came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger” (Luk 2:16). Solomon had said, “where no oxen are, the crib is clean” (Pro 14:4) — a clean crib is an empty barn, and the LORD came not to a clean world but to a foul one, into the smell and straw of it. This is the condescension of Christ, measured in inches: He who filled heaven was laid in a box a yard long, and He who is the Bread of life was laid where the food is put.
webster_summary: A trough or crib from which cattle eat; the place where the newborn Christ was laid, and the angel’s appointed sign.
webster_full: MANGER, a trough or box in which fodder is laid for cattle to eat.
From the Old French manger, “to eat,” and the Latin manducare, “to chew.”
It renders the Greek phatnē, the feeding-place of the stalled beasts.
There the newborn Christ was laid, for there was no room in the inn (Luk 2:7).
It was made the sign by which the shepherds should know Him (Luk 2:12).
scriptures: Luk 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Luk 2:12
And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
Luk 2:16
And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger.
Pro 14:4
Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox.
corruption_summary: The sentimentalized, de-historicized Christmas keeps the manger and loses the incarnate God who was laid in it in order to die.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a real corruption here, and it is affectionate rather than hostile, which makes it harder to shake. The age has kept the manger and lost the Christ. It has made the scene a tableau — a hushed barn, a soft light, a baby who never cries and never grows — and it has quietly moved the whole thing out of history into the safe country of story, where nothing is required of anyone. That drift runs on two rails. The first is sentiment, which loves the crib and will not look toward Calvary. The second is a de-historicizing habit that treats the nativity as a devotional legend rather than an event Luke dated, located, and researched, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first. Luke wrote history. There was a census, a town, a trough, and a boy born in it.

The manger is not a nursery ornament; it is the first inch of the descent that ends at the cross. He was laid in the cattle’s feeding-box because there was no room, and He would die outside the gate because there was no room; the whole life is bracketed by the world’s refusal. He who made the beasts that fed at that trough was laid in it; He who is the Bread of life was set down where the food is put; and He came, being rich, to be poor, that we through His poverty might be rich. Take the deity out of the manger and there is nothing left but a poor family in a bad night’s lodging — touching, and no gospel at all. Keep the deity in it, and the crib becomes the most staggering fact in the world: God, in flesh, in the straw, on His way to die for His people.
roots_summary: The word means a feeding-trough, the crib out of which cattle eat.
roots_lines: Manger — Old French mangeoire, “an eating-place.”
From manger, “to eat,” from Latin manducare, “to chew.”
It renders the Greek phatnē, the trough of the stalled beasts.
Solomon’s “crib” is the same furniture: clean only where no oxen are (Pro 14:4).
In it the newborn Christ was laid, and by it He was known (Luk 2:12).
usage: The Bread of life was laid where the food is put — God in flesh, in the cattle’s crib.
The angel gave a trough for a sign: you shall know the Christ of God by a manger.
Where no oxen are, the crib is clean; He came not to a clean world but to a foul one.

etymology: From the Middle English swathel, “a bandage, a swathe,” from Old English sweþel, akin to swathe, “to bind about”; the long strips of cloth in which a newborn was wound close to the body. It renders the Greek verb sparganoo', “to wrap in bands.”
biblical_def: Swaddling clothes are the narrow bands in which a newborn child was wound — long strips of cloth passed about the limbs and body to hold them straight and warm, the ordinary, tender, unremarkable care of every mother in Israel. To be swaddled was the mark of a child received and cherished. Ezekiel makes the point by its absence: he pictures Jerusalem as a foundling on the day of her birth, whose navel was not cut, who was not washed, not salted, “nor swaddled at all” (Eze 16:4) — a baby left in the open field to die, until the LORD passed by and said, Live. That is the background against which Luke writes. Mary “brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes” (Luk 2:7). The eternal Son, by whom all things were made and by whom all things consist, submitted to being bound in bands and laid down where He was put. He could not lift His head; His hands, which had stretched out the heavens, were wrapped fast by His mother. And the angel gave the bands themselves as the sign: “ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes” (Luk 2:12). Here is real flesh, real infancy, real dependence — no phantom, no appearance of a body, but a true man with a soul and a body, who made Himself of no reputation, and took upon Him the form of a servant (Php 2:7). The bands of Bethlehem look toward the graveclothes of Jerusalem: He was bound at both ends of His life for us.
webster_summary: The bands or strips of cloth in which a newborn child was wound about; the sign by which the shepherds knew the Christ.
webster_full: SWADDLING CLOTHES, cloths or bands wrapped about a newborn infant.
From swathe, “to bind about,” Old English sweþel, a bandage.
They render the Greek sparganoo', “to wrap in swaddling bands.”
To be swaddled was the token of a child received and cared for (Eze 16:4).
Mary wrapped the newborn Christ in them, and they were made the angel’s sign (Luk 2:7, 12).
scriptures: Luk 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Luk 2:12
And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
Eze 16:4
And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
corruption_summary: The sentimental Christmas keeps the bands and loses the God who wore them; the bands themselves rebuke every denial of Christ’s true flesh.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the Christmas that keeps the swaddling bands as decoration and drops the doctrine they carry. The scene is retold every December as warmth and family and a gentle infant, and it is emptied in the telling of the one thing that makes it worth telling: that the child in those bands is God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, who was born to die. A nativity without the deity of the babe is a poor lodging-house anecdote. A nativity without the cross is a story with no reason in it. He was wrapped in bands at Bethlehem and in graveclothes at Jerusalem, and the first wrapping was for the sake of the second.

The bands rebuke an older error as well, and one that keeps creeping back: the Docetic instinct that will grant Christ a seeming body but not a real one. Docetism was named and rejected in the ancient church, and Chalcedon settled the matter — one Person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The swaddling clothes are the plain evidence. A phantom does not need binding; an appearance is not wound in strips of cloth by its mother’s hands. Ezekiel’s unswaddled foundling shows what the bands mean: to be swaddled is to be received, owned, cared for. The Son of God took a true body, in a true infancy, in true helplessness, and made Himself of no reputation. If He was not truly man He cannot stand in our room; if He was not truly God His obedience cannot avail for a multitude. The bands say He was both.
roots_summary: The words mean the bands of cloth in which a newborn was wound about and bound.
roots_lines: Swaddle — Middle English swathel, “a bandage,” akin to swathe.
From Old English sweþel, a band for binding about.
It renders the Greek sparganoo', “to wrap in swaddling bands.”
The unswaddled infant was the cast-out foundling (Eze 16:4).
The swaddled babe was the angel’s appointed sign (Luk 2:12).
usage: The hands that stretched out the heavens were wrapped fast in bands by His mother.
Ezekiel’s foundling was not swaddled at all: to be swaddled is to be received and owned.
Bound in bands at Bethlehem, bound in graveclothes at Jerusalem — He was bound for us.

etymology: From the Old English sopp, akin to sūpan, “to sup, to soak”; a morsel of bread dipped in liquid. It renders the Greek psōmion, “a little piece, a morsel,” the KJV margin giving “morsel.”
biblical_def: A sop is a morsel of bread dipped in the dish — in the East, the host’s own hand taking a piece, wetting it in the broth or charoseth, and passing it to a guest. It was a courtesy, and more: the sop given by the master of the feast was a mark of singular favour, reserved for a friend at the table. That is the whole weight of John 13. The Lord is troubled in spirit and testifies that one of them shall betray Him; and when John asks who, “Jesus answered, He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon” (Joh 13:26). Christ knew the man, named the deed, and then handed him the morsel of honour — the last courtesy of the covenant table extended to the traitor’s own hand. He had already quoted the psalm over him: “He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me” (Joh 13:18; Psa 41:9). Nothing more could be offered; the kindness had run to its end. “And after the sop Satan entered into him. Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly” (Joh 13:27). The morsel that should have melted him hardened him. Mercy refused is not neutral: the same sun that softens the wax bakes the clay. Judas ate from the Saviour’s hand and went out, and it was night.
webster_summary: A morsel of bread dipped in the dish; the host’s token of favour, given by Christ to Judas at the table.
webster_full: SOP, a piece of bread or other food dipped or soaked in liquid.
From the Old English sopp, akin to sūpan, “to sup, to soak.”
It renders the Greek psōmion; the KJV margin gives “morsel.”
For the master of a feast to dip and give the sop was a mark of favour to a guest.
Christ gave the sop to Judas Iscariot, and after the sop Satan entered into him (Joh 13:26-27).
scriptures: Jesus answered, He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.
And after the sop Satan entered into him. Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly.
I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.
Psa 41:9
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
corruption_summary: The Gnostic rehabilitation of Judas — revived with much noise from the so-called Gospel of Judas — recasts the traitor as the enlightened insider; the sop refutes it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the rehabilitation of Judas. The so-called Gospel of Judas is a second-century Sethian Gnostic forgery, no part of the sixty-six-book canon, which inverts the account and makes the betrayer the one disciple who truly understood — and it was paraded before the public in 2006 as though a buried truth had surfaced. It has an appetite behind it: an age that dislikes the category of the reprobate would rather have a misunderstood Judas, a tragic instrument, a man more sinned against than sinning. John gives no such quarter. He tells us plainly that Judas was a thief and had the bag; that Christ knew from the beginning who should betray Him; that the psalm was fulfilled in the man who ate His bread and lifted up the heel. Gnostic forgeries do not correct the apostles.

The sop itself is the answer, and it is more terrible than any theory. Christ dipped the morsel and put it into the traitor’s hand — the host’s courtesy, the token of a friend at the table, offered to the man already bargaining for silver. Judas had heard every sermon, seen every miracle, carried the bag, had his feet washed by the Lord that very hour, and took the last kindness from His fingers; and after the sop, Satan entered into him. Here is the doctrine the age cannot bear: nearness to Christ is not grace, and privilege refused becomes hardness. The same morsel that would have broken a believing heart sealed a treacherous one. Let no man rest in his seat at the table, his membership, or his labours for the church, who has never come to Christ himself. Judas went out from the covenant supper, and it was night.
roots_summary: The word means a morsel of bread dipped in the dish and given by the host.
roots_lines: Sop — Old English sopp, akin to sūpan, “to sup, to soak.”
It denotes a morsel of bread dipped or soaked in liquid.
It renders the Greek psōmion, “a little piece”; the margin: “morsel.”
For the host to dip and give the sop was a token of favour to a guest.
After the sop, Satan entered into Judas (Joh 13:27).
usage: Christ dipped the sop and gave it to Judas — the last courtesy of the table to the traitor.
He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me: the psalm named the man.
After the sop, Satan entered in — mercy refused hardens; nearness to Christ is not grace.

etymology: From the Old English sceamol, “a bench, a stool,” from the Latin scamellum, a little bench — hence the butcher’s bench, the stall on which flesh was cut and sold, and so the meat market itself. It renders the Greek makellon. The modern sense of “a scene of ruin” is a later drift from the slaughter-house.
biblical_def: The shambles is the meat market — the butchers’ row, the benches where flesh was cut and sold in a Greek city. In Corinth this was no simple errand. Much of the meat on those benches had been offered first at a heathen altar, the priest taking his portion and the surplus going to the stalls; a Christian housewife buying a joint might well be buying what had lain before an idol that morning. Paul settles it in one line: “whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof” (1Co 10:25-26). The ground of the liberty is not indifference but doctrine. An idol is nothing in the world; the beef was never Apollo’s; it was always God’s, for the earth is His and everything in it, and no demon can annex a creature the LORD has made and pronounced good. Buy it, thank God for it, and eat. But Paul does not stop at liberty. If a man tell thee, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not — not for thine own conscience, but for the other man’s: “Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other” (1Co 10:29). The strong man’s freedom bends before the weak brother’s scruple, for the same apostle who says all things are lawful says all things edify not. Liberty is real, and it is never sovereign; it is a servant, and love is its master.
webster_summary: The butchers’ benches; the meat market, where flesh offered to idols was commonly sold.
webster_full: SHAMBLES, the benches or stalls on which butchers expose flesh for sale; a meat market.
From the Old English sceamol, a bench, from the Latin scamellum.
It renders the Greek makellon, the provision market of a Greek city.
In Corinth much of its meat had first been offered at a heathen altar.
Paul bids the Christian buy and eat, asking no question for conscience sake (1Co 10:25).
scriptures: Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake:
For the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof.
Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other: for why is my liberty judged of another man's conscience?
I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean.
corruption_summary: The age has made conscience sovereign and liberty an end in itself; Paul makes conscience answerable to Scripture and liberty a servant of love.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a genuine redefinition here, and it turns on the word conscience. Paul’s conscience is a faculty that must be informed by revelation and can be wrongly bound or wrongly loosed; the age’s conscience is the autonomous self, and “follow your conscience” has come to mean that whatever a man sincerely feels is thereby right and beyond correction. That is not the apostle’s doctrine. He tells the Corinthians why they may eat — because the earth is the Lord’s and the fulness thereof, and an idol is nothing in the world — and the reason is a truth outside the man, not a feeling inside him. A conscience is a window, not a lamp. Scripture alone binds it absolutely; where Scripture has spoken, sincerity is no defence, and where Scripture is silent, no man may forge a chain for his brother.

The shambles cuts both ways, and the church has always been tempted to fall off one side or the other. Legalism looks at the butcher’s bench and forbids what God has not forbidden, making rules where the LORD made meat, and it insults the Creator by conceding to a nothing-idol what belongs to Him. License looks at the same bench, hears the true word that all things are lawful, and marches off to eat in the idol’s temple with a weak brother watching — and so, for a plate of beef, destroys him for whom Christ died. Paul refuses both. Buy in the shambles and ask no questions; but if a man tells you where the meat has been, and his conscience is troubled, put down your fork. The liberty is real and dearly bought, and it is held in trust for the good of the brethren, not spent upon ourselves.
roots_summary: The word means the butchers’ benches, the market where flesh was sold.
roots_lines: Shambles — Old English sceamol, “a bench,” from Latin scamellum.
It denotes the butcher’s stall, and so the meat market itself.
It renders the Greek makellon, the provision market (1Co 10:25).
In Corinth its flesh had commonly been offered first to idols.
The later sense of “a scene of ruin” drifted from the slaughter-house.
usage: Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat — for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof.
The idol never owned the beef; a nothing cannot annex what God pronounced good.
If the weak brother’s conscience is told, put down the fork: liberty serves love, and never rules it.

etymology: From husband in its older sense — Old Norse hūsbōndi, “master of a house” — whence “to husband”, to till and manage; hence a tiller of the ground, a farmer, a vinedresser. It renders the Greek geōrgos, “a worker of the earth.”
biblical_def: A husbandman is a tiller of the ground — a farmer, a keeper of vines and fields, one who works the earth and waits on it. The word has nothing to do with marriage; a husbandman husbands the soil. Scripture puts it to three uses. It is a figure of patience: “the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain” (Jas 5:7) — he cannot hasten a harvest, and neither may the saint hasten the coming of the Lord. It is a figure of the labourer’s right: “the husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits” (2Ti 2:6). And it is the figure of judgment: the householder let out his vineyard “to husbandmen, and went into a far country” (Mat 21:33), and those wicked tenants beat the servants and at last killed the son, saying, This is the heir; let us seize on his inheritance. But the word is crowned in the upper room. “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman” (Joh 15:1). The Father Himself is the Vinedresser, and He is not an absentee. “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” (Joh 15:2). His care is definite, personal, and effectual: He knows the vine, He knows every branch of it, and He has never yet lost one that was truly in the Son.
webster_summary: A tiller of the ground; a farmer or vinedresser; in John 15 the Father Himself, who prunes the branches of the true Vine.
webster_full: HUSBANDMAN, one who tills the ground; a farmer; a cultivator of vines and fields.
From husband in the old sense of the master of a house, whence “to husband,” to till and manage.
It renders the Greek geōrgos, “a worker of the earth.”
The husbandman waiteth with long patience for the precious fruit (Jas 5:7).
“My Father is the husbandman” — the Vinedresser of the true Vine (Joh 15:1).
scriptures: Joh 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Joh 15:2
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.

Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:
Jas 5:7

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition presses on the word; it recovers the Father’s pruning knife and His definite, effectual care of every branch in the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: The live temptation is to resent the knife. The husbandman of John 15 does not merely admire His vine; He cuts it. Every branch that beareth fruit, He purgeth — and the pruning falls not on the barren wood but on the fruitful, precisely because it is fruitful and He means to have more. The soul under that blade will always be tempted to read the affliction as neglect or as cruelty, and to conclude that a Father who loved would leave the vine alone. He would not. A vine left alone runs to leaf and gives no wine. The believer who is being cut back is not being cast off; he is being tended by a Husbandman who is far more interested in his fruit than he is himself, and who never makes a stroke that is not needed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the definiteness of the Father’s care. He does not tend vineyards in general; He tends this Vine, and every branch in it, by name. The wicked husbandmen of Matthew 21 show the alternative — tenants who treated the vineyard as their own, beat the servants, and killed the heir to seize the inheritance, and were destroyed. But the true Vine has a true Husbandman, and His work is effectual: what He plants lives, what He purges bears, and the branch that abides in Christ shall bring forth much fruit, because the Vinedresser has purposed it. Then let the saint be as patient with God as the farmer is with his field, waiting for the early and the latter rain, and knowing that the hand which holds the knife is the hand of his Father.
roots_summary: The word means a tiller of the ground — a farmer, a keeper of vines.
roots_lines: Husbandman — from husband, Old Norse hūsbōndi, “master of a house.”
Hence “to husband”: to till, to manage, to keep. It has no reference to marriage.
It renders the Greek geōrgos, “a worker of the earth.”
It denotes the farmer, the vinedresser, the tenant of a vineyard (Mat 21:33).
The Father is the Husbandman of the true Vine (Joh 15:1).
usage: My Father is the husbandman: the Vinedresser is no absentee, and He knows every branch.
He purgeth the fruitful branch — the knife falls on the living wood, that it bear more.
The husbandman waiteth with long patience for the early and the latter rain.

etymology: From the Greek iōta, the name of the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, answering to the Hebrew yodh — the least character in the Hebrew square script, a mere stroke no bigger than a comma; hence the smallest possible particle of writing, and so of anything.
biblical_def: A jot is the smallest letter there is — the Hebrew yodh, a single stroke hardly larger than an apostrophe, the least mark a scribe’s pen can set down. Our Lord chose it deliberately. Having declared, “Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil” (Mat 5:17), He measures the law’s permanence by its tiniest character: “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). Luke keeps the same balance: “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail” (Luk 16:17). Set the two halves of that scale side by side and the weight of it is staggering. On the one side, the whole created order — the mountains, the seas, the sun and the stars. On the other, one stroke of one letter of the Hebrew Bible. And the stars will go first. This is verbal plenary inspiration from the lips of Christ Himself: not the ideas of Scripture only, nor its themes, nor its general drift, but its very words, down to the least letter of the least word, are the breath of God and cannot fail. The psalmist had said it already: “For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven” (Psa 119:89). The Book is not a record of men’s reaching toward God; it is God’s speech, and He does not misspeak, and He does not lose a letter of it.
webster_summary: The Greek iota, answering to the Hebrew yodh — the smallest letter of the alphabet; hence the least particle of anything.
webster_full: JOT, the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, iota; the Hebrew yodh.
In the Hebrew square script the yodh is a single small stroke.
Hence, the least point or particle; the smallest imaginable quantity.
Not one jot shall pass from the law till all be fulfilled (Mat 5:18).
It is the measure Christ chose for the permanence of God’s written word.
scriptures: Mat 5:17
Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Mat 5:18
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail.
LAMED. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven.
corruption_summary: The denial of inerrancy — the modernist and higher-critical dismantling of the text into sources, layers, and late accretions — is foreclosed by Christ’s own doctrine of the jot.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the denial of inerrancy, and it comes to us with a pedigree. Nineteenth-century German higher criticism, and its heirs down to the present, taught the church to hold the Bible at arm’s length: to carve the Torah into a documentary hypothesis of imagined sources, to invent a second and third Isaiah, to date what was early as though it were late, and to reclassify the Bible’s history as legendary material — and then to assure the faithful that the essence of Scripture survives untouched, since only the words are in question. Christ has foreclosed the whole enterprise. He did not say that the substance of the law abides, or its spirit, or its enduring principles. He said that not one jot — not one stroke of one letter — shall in no wise pass, till all be fulfilled. If the least letter cannot fail, the layers and the redactors and the late accretions have nowhere to stand.

Weigh the scale our Lord set up. Heaven and earth on one side; a single Hebrew yodh on the other; and Luke says it is the easier thing for heaven and earth to go. That is the dictionary’s doctrine of Scripture in one sentence from the mouth of the Son of God: verbal, plenary inspiration — every word, in all its parts, God-breathed, inerrant and infallible in the original autographs, and providentially preserved to His church. The consequence is practical and searching. If the words are God’s, then a man may not pick among them, nor keep the commands he finds congenial and lose the rest in the shuffle of scholarship; and Christ goes straight from the jot to the sixth and seventh commandments, driving them into the heart. He who would not let one letter fall will not let one commandment fall either. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven — and what is settled there is not open for revision here.
roots_summary: The word means the smallest letter of the alphabet — the Greek iota, the Hebrew yodh.
roots_lines: Jot — from the Greek iōta, the least letter of that alphabet.
It answers to the Hebrew yodh, a single small stroke of the pen.
Hence it denotes the least particle, the smallest imaginable part.
Christ measured the law’s permanence by it (Mat 5:18).
Heaven and earth shall pass before one jot of the word shall fail (Luk 16:17).
usage: One jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law — the stars will go first.
Christ measures the word by its smallest letter: the very words are God-breathed, not the drift only.
For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven — and what is settled there is not open for revision.
